stimulus.source_note: Platt Amendment, Army Appropriations Act, approved March 2, 1901, public domain (abridged).
stimulus.text: "Article III. The Government of Cuba consents that the United States may exercise the right to intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence, the maintenance of a government adequate for the protection of life, property, and individual liberty, and for discharging the obligations with respect to Cuba imposed by the Treaty of Paris on the United States. . . . Article VII. To enable the United States to maintain the independence of Cuba, and to protect the people thereof, as well as for its own defense, the Government of Cuba will sell or lease to the United States lands necessary for coaling or naval stations, at certain specified points, to be agreed upon with the President of the United States." — Platt Amendment, March 2, 1901 (abridged)

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim abridged excerpt from the Platt Amendment, March 2, 1901, public domain
stem: Under Article III, the United States reserved the right to

options.text: Annex Cuba and make it an American territory whenever it chose
options.misconception: Article III allows intervention, not annexation; the United States never annexed Cuba.

options.text: Intervene in Cuba to preserve independence and protect life, property, and liberty

options.misconception: Nothing in Article III taxes sugar; it is about intervention to preserve independence and order.
The amendment allows intervention when needed, not a permanent garrison in the capital.

rationales.A: Intervention is not annexation. The amendment keeps Cuba nominally independent while reserving American control.
rationales.B: Article III says the United States may intervene for the preservation of Cuban independence and a government that protects life, property, and liberty.
rationales.C: Sugar taxes appear nowhere in the article. The right reserved is intervention, not taxation.
rationales.D: The article reserves a right to step in, not a permanent post. American troops left Cuba in 1902.
rationales.general:
1. Read Article III slowly. Cuba consents that the United States may exercise the right to intervene.
2. Note the purposes. Intervention is for preserving Cuban independence and a government that protects life, property, and liberty.
3. Rule out the rest. Annexation, taxes, and permanent troops are all stronger than what the article claims.
Remember: a right to step in is not a right to stay, so read the limits as carefully as the power.
